literal: Fan Ban, General Who Breaks the Enemy and Marquis of Guangwu;
idiomatic: Fan Ban held the rank of General Who Breaks the Enemy and Marquis of Guangwu;

literal: Jia Qing, General Who Establishes Martial and Marquis of Shangluo;
idiomatic: Jia Qing was General Who Establishes Martial and Marquis of Shangluo;

literal: Jia Xun, Commandery Marquis;
idiomatic: Jia Xun held commandery marquis rank;

literal: Li Yi, Marquis of Guanzhong;
idiomatic: Li Yi was enfeoffed Marquis of Guanzhong;

literal: Guo Ru, Marquis Within the Passes.
idiomatic: Guo Ru held the title Marquis Within the Passes.

literal: All were enfeoffed and appointed by tables from Emperor Huan.
idiomatic: Each had received rank and title from Emperor Huan's commendations.

literal: In the trouble of Six Xiu, most of those who survived followed Liu Kun's heir-son Ziyun in flight south.
idiomatic: After the Six Xiu disaster, most survivors fled south with Ren Ziyun, Liu Kun's designated heir.

literal: The names of Wei Xiong, Ji Dan, Mo Han, and others all appear on the stele.
idiomatic: Wei Xiong, Ji Dan, Mo Han, and others are all named on the monument.

literal: Xiong's style was Shiyuan, Dan's style Shiya; both were brave and strong and full of stratagems, Jin-era provincial aides.
idiomatic: Xiong styled himself Shiyuan and Dan Shiya; both were bold, resourceful men who had served as provincial aides under the Jin.

literal: After they entered the state together with Wei Cao, Emperor Huan admired their physical strength and made them both generals; they constantly followed on campaign and won great renown.
idiomatic: When they entered the realm with Wei Cao, Emperor Huan was impressed by their strength and made them generals; they fought at his side on campaign after campaign and won a towering reputation.

literal: When Emperor Huan went to relieve the crisis, he memorialized the Jin court listing their achievements, and all were appointed generals.
idiomatic: When Emperor Huan marched to the rescue, he reported their deeds to the Jin court and secured general's commissions for them all.

literal: Xiong repeatedly won in battle and was gradually promoted to Left General and Marquis of Yunzhong.
idiomatic: Xiong piled victory on victory until he rose to Left General and Marquis of Yunzhong.

literal: Dan too was famed for courage in action; at the end of Emperor Huan's reign he reached General of Faith and Righteousness and Marquis of Loufan.
idiomatic: Dan likewise became famous for martial feats; by the close of Emperor Huan's reign he held General of Faith and Righteousness and Marquis of Loufan.

literal: At the beginning of Emperor Mu's reign both were entrusted with office.
idiomatic: Early in Emperor Mu's reign both were again given weighty trust.

literal: After Wei Cao died, both became left and right assisting ministers.
idiomatic: After Wei Cao's death they served together as the left and right hands of government.

literal: In the rebellion of Six Xiu the state fell into great disorder; old and new factions nursed suspicion and slaughtered one another in turn.
idiomatic: The Six Xiu revolt threw the realm into chaos; old settlers and new allies eyed one another with suspicion and killed in waves.

literal: Xiong and Dan were both attached to by the multitude; they plotted to flee south and said to the assembly: "We hear the old hands resent the newcomers' fierceness in battle and mean to kill them all; if we do not plan early, I fear our line will perish.
idiomatic: The crowd rallied to Xiong and Dan; they planned a southern flight and told the assembly, "We hear the old faction hates how fiercely the newcomers fight and intends to wipe them out. Unless we act now, our line will end."

literal: " Jin men and Wuhuan were alarmed and afraid, and all said: "Death follows the two generals.
idiomatic: " Jin subjects and Wuhuan alike were terrified and cried, "We live or die with these two generals."

literal: " Thereupon Xiong and Dan with Liu Kun's heir-son Ziyun led tens of thousands of Wuhuan and Jin men in revolt.
idiomatic: " Then Xiong and Dan, with Ren Ziyun, Liu Kun's heir, led tens of thousands of Wuhuan and Jin followers into open revolt.

literal: Kun heard and was greatly pleased; he led several hundred horsemen at full gallop to Pingcheng to receive and comfort them.
idiomatic: Liu Kun was overjoyed at the news and raced to Pingcheng with a few hundred horsemen to welcome and settle them.

literal: It happened that Shi Le attacked Kun's Le'ping; the prefect Han Ju requested rescue from Kun.
idiomatic: Just then Shi Le struck Liu Kun at Le'ping; the prefect Han Ju begged Liu Kun for relief.

literal: Kun, having gained the hosts of Xiong and Dan, wished to use their sharp edge to destroy Shi Le.
idiomatic: Liu Kun, now reinforced by Xiong and Dan's troops, meant to hurl that fresh strength against Shi Le and destroy him.

literal: Xiong and Dan remonstrated, saying: "The disorderly masses are hungry and weary and cannot yet be used; it is fit to rest, watch for openings, and then move.
idiomatic: Xiong and Dan urged caution: "These men are hungry, exhausted rebels—not yet fit to throw into battle. Rest them, watch for an opening, then strike."

literal: " Kun would not follow; he sent Xiong and Dan to lead the host against Le; Kun encamped at Guangmu to sound support.
idiomatic: " Liu Kun refused. He sent Xiong and Dan against Le while he held Guangmu to back them.

literal: Le led light cavalry to battle Xiong and Dan; Dan was utterly defeated and fled with more than a thousand horsemen to Dai commandery.
idiomatic: Shi Le met them with light cavalry; Dan was routed and fled north with a thousand riders into Dai.

literal: Le sent Kong Chang in pursuit to destroy him.
idiomatic: Le sent Kong Chang in pursuit to finish him off.

literal: Mo Han was a man of Fanzhi in Yanmen.
idiomatic: Mo Han came from Fanzhi in Yanmen.

literal: His family for generations traded goods and amassed wealth in the tens of millions.
idiomatic: His family had traded for generations and piled up wealth beyond counting.

literal: When Liu Kun held Bing province he summoned Han as an aide.
idiomatic: When Liu Kun governed Bingzhou he took Han on as an aide.

literal: Han dwelt near the frontier and often came and went within the state.
idiomatic: Han lived near the border and often traveled into the Tuoba realm.

literal: Emperor Mu loved his talent and capacity and treated him well.
idiomatic: Emperor Mu admired his ability and treated him generously.

literal: When he became Prince of Dai he fully set up officials and sought Han from Kun.
idiomatic: When he became Prince of Dai he formed a full court and asked Liu Kun to send Han to him.

literal: Kun sent him into the state; Han in his heart was unwilling.
idiomatic: Liu Kun sent him, but Han's heart was not in the move.

literal: Kun instructed him, saying: "Today the Hu raiders fill the sky, extinguishing the various Xia; the hundred surnames are displaced, death covers the ground, the sovereign is held in secret imprisonment, drowned among ugly captors.
idiomatic: Liu Kun reasoned with him: "Barbarian armies now cover the sky and are snuffing out the Chinese realms; the people wander homeless, the roads are heaped with dead, and our emperor languishes in the hands of savage captors."

literal: Only this one province stands among the mass of Hu; that I, with my slight virtue, can preserve myself and stand upright is because I rely on the Prince of Dai's strength.
idiomatic: " Only this province still stands amid the barbarian tide; that I survive at all on my meager merit is because the Prince of Dai upholds me."

literal: Therefore I pour out body and treasure, send my eldest son far as hostage, and hope to extinguish the remnant bandits and wash away the great shame.
idiomatic: " I have poured out my person and my wealth, sent my eldest son away as hostage, and staked everything on crushing the remnant enemy and avenging the realm's disgrace."

literal: You, as a man of loyal integrity, are also in a time to rouse righteousness; how can you be sparing of a small bond of service together and forget the great benefit of your own emergence?
idiomatic: " You are a man of loyalty; this is the hour to act on it. How can you cling to a petty tie of service and forget the far greater good of stepping forward?"

literal: To enter and become the Prince of Dai's trusted center is not only my wish but also what one province relies upon.
idiomatic: " To enter and become the prince's trusted confidant is not only my wish—it is what our whole province depends on."

literal: " Han then entered Dai and took part in state office.
idiomatic: " Han at last entered Dai and joined the government.

literal: Later Kun moved the people of five counties south of the Xing ridge; Han's household alone remained.
idiomatic: Later Liu Kun relocated five counties' people south of the Xing Mountains; Han's family alone stayed behind.

literal: Han was greatly valued by Emperor Mu and constantly took part in great plans of army and state.
idiomatic: Emperor Mu held him in the highest regard and kept him at the heart of military and civil strategy.

literal: He died in office as Left General and Marquis of Guanzhong.
idiomatic: He died holding Left General and Marquis of Guanzhong.

literal: His old residence lay south of the Sanggan River; the world calls it Mo Han's rampart, or through corrupted pronunciation Mo Hui City.
idiomatic: His old house stood south of the Sanggan River; people still call the place Mo Han's Rampart—or, in a corrupted pronunciation, Mo Hui City.

literal: His son Xian was famed in the age.
idiomatic: His son Xian won renown in his own day.

literal: In the Zhaocheng era he was made Left Palace Attendant.
idiomatic: Under Emperor Zhaocheng he became Left Palace Attendant.

literal: Xian's son Ti also had stratagems.
idiomatic: Xian's son Ti was likewise a man of counsel.

literal: Taizu sent Ti with the general Wang Jian and the three armies to campaign against Murong Bao's Guangning prefect Liu Kangqi and beheaded him.
idiomatic: Taizu sent Ti with General Wang Jian and a three-wing army against Murong Bao's Guangning prefect Liu Kangqi and took his head.

literal: Kangqi's tribes were moved to Pingcheng.
idiomatic: Kangqi's tribes were resettled at Pingcheng.

literal: Bao's Shanggu prefect Lin abandoned the commandery and fled; Taizu pursued in punishment; Ti was made grand general and marched out by the eastern route.
idiomatic: Bao's Shanggu prefect Lin deserted his commandery and fled; Taizu pursued him; Ti was made grand general and took a separate eastern road.

literal: For merit he was given the enfeoffment Marquis of Dongwan.
idiomatic: For his merit he was enfeoffed Marquis of Dongwan.

literal: When he returned to the capital he constantly attended banquets with Li Li.
idiomatic: Back at the capital he often shared the emperor's table with Li Li.

literal: Li was punished for irreverence in seating; Ti was also demoted to Administrator of Jiyang.
idiomatic: Li was punished for disrespect at court; Ti was demoted as well, to administrator of Jiyang.

literal: Later Taizu wished to enlarge the palaces and measured several tens of li around Pingcheng, intending to model Ye, Luoyang, and Chang'an; timber in the millions of logs was transported.
idiomatic: Later Taizu planned to expand the palace quarter, surveyed dozens of li around Pingcheng, and meant to imitate Ye, Luoyang, and Chang'an; millions of timbers were hauled in.

literal: Because Ti was ingenious in mechanism he was summoned and ordered to supervise.
idiomatic: Ti's mechanical ingenuity won him summons to oversee the work.

literal: He was called in and discussed the fitness of the construction.
idiomatic: He was called in to debate the right scale and design of the build.

literal: Ti after long attendance grew somewhat slack; he was granted death.
idiomatic: After long attendance Ti grew careless in his duties and was put to death.

literal: Ti's younger brother Yun loved learning and was skilled at archery.
idiomatic: Ti's younger brother Yun loved books and excelled at the bow.

literal: In Taizu's time he constantly managed the Selection Bureau and was transferred to Palace Attendant.
idiomatic: Under Taizu he ran the Selection Bureau and later became palace attendant.

literal: For merit he was given the enfeoffment Marquis of Ande.
idiomatic: For merit he was enfeoffed Marquis of Ande.

literal: He was promoted Commandant of Cavalry and constantly took part in deliberations on army and state.
idiomatic: He rose to Commandant of Cavalry and sat in on every major counsel of war and state.

literal: When Shizu captured Helian Chang, he edicted Yun and the Prince of Changshan Su to remain and garrison Tongwan.
idiomatic: When Shizu took Helian Chang, he ordered Yun and Prince Su of Changshan to hold Tongwan.

literal: His rank was advanced to Duke of Anding, with added General Who Pacifies the West; later he was transferred Grand General Who Guards the West.
idiomatic: He was raised to Duke of Anding and General Who Pacifies the West, then to Grand General Who Guards the West.

literal: At that time the Hexi region had just been annexed and hearts were not yet one; Yun comforted old and new alike and all found their place.
idiomatic: The Hexi had only just been absorbed and loyalties were still divided; Yun soothed old subjects and new until each settled where he belonged.

literal: He died in the Shenju era; posthumous title: Duke Reverent.
idiomatic: He died in the Shenju era and was posthumously titled Duke Reverent.

literal: Liu Kuren, original style Meigen, was of the lineage of Liu Hu; he had another name, Lo Chui.
idiomatic: Liu Kuren, whose original name was Meigen, belonged to the house of Liu Hu and was also called Lo Chui.

literal: In youth he was bold and open, with wisdom and stratagem.
idiomatic: As a young man he was open-handed and bold, with a strategist's mind.

literal: His mother was a daughter of Emperor Pingwen.
idiomatic: His mother was born a princess of Emperor Pingwen's house.

literal: Emperor Zhaocheng again gave him a clanswoman in marriage and made him southern grandee.
idiomatic: Emperor Zhaocheng married him to another royal clanswoman and made him southern grandee.

literal: In the thirty-ninth year of Jianguo Emperor Zhaocheng died suddenly; Taizu was not yet established; Fu Jian made Kuren General Who Commands the River and Marquis Within the Passes and ordered him with Wei Chen to divide the state's tribes and rule them.
idiomatic: In Jianguo year 39 Emperor Zhaocheng died suddenly before Taizu could be enthroned; Fu Jian made Liu Kuren General Who Commands the River and Marquis Within the Passes and set him with Wei Chen to divide and govern the tribal following.

literal: From the river west belonged to Wei Chen; from the river east belonged to Kuren.
idiomatic: West of the river fell to Wei Chen; east of the river to Liu Kuren.

literal: Thereupon the Empress Dowager Xianming brought Taizu and the two princes of Wei and Qin from the Helan tribe to dwell there.
idiomatic: Then Empress Dowager Xianming brought Taizu and the Wei and Qin princes from the Helan tribe to live under Kuren's protection.

literal: Kuren served with full loyalty and did not change his constancy with rise or fall; he gathered and settled the scattered, and his favor and trust were greatly manifest.
idiomatic: Liu Kuren served him with unwavering loyalty, never shifting with fortune's turns; he gathered the scattered and won them with grace, and his trustworthiness was plain to all.

literal: Fu Jian advanced Kuren to General of Guangwu, gave him banner, canopy, drums, and parasol, and ceremonial parity with feudal lords.
idiomatic: Fu Jian promoted him to General of Guangwu and granted the insignia of banner, canopy, drums, and parasol, with ceremony equal to a feudal lord.

literal: Wei Chen was placed below Kuren.
idiomatic: Wei Chen was ranked beneath Liu Kuren.

literal: Wei Chen was enraged, killed Fu Jian's Administrator of Wuyuan, and rebelled, attacking Kuren's western territory.
idiomatic: Wei Chen flew into rage, murdered Fu Jian's administrator of Wuyuan, rebelled, and struck Liu Kuren's western lands.

literal: Kuren again campaigned against Wei Chen and defeated him, pursuing to more than a thousand li northwest of Yin Mountain, taking his wife and children and gathering all his followers.
idiomatic: Liu Kuren counterattacked, broke Wei Chen, and chased him more than a thousand li beyond Yin Mountain, seizing his family and absorbing his entire following.

literal: Kuren campaigned west against the Kudi tribe, took great herds and goods, moved their tribes, and settled them on the Sanggan River.
idiomatic: He marched west against the Kudi, captured vast herds, relocated the tribe, and planted them along the Sanggan.

literal: Fu Jian bestowed on Kuren's wife the Gongsun clan and enriched her dowry and gifts.
idiomatic: Fu Jian gave Liu Kuren's wife the surname Gongsun and loaded her with gifts.

literal: Kuren again went to Jian and was further made General Who Quells Might.
idiomatic: Liu Kuren went again to Fu Jian's court and was raised to General Who Quells Might.

literal: Later Murong Chui besieged Fu Pi at Ye and also sent a general, Ping Gui, to attack Fu Jian's Inspector of Youzhou Wang Yong at Ji; Kuren, holding himself bound by the titles Jian had granted, sent his wife's elder brother Gongsun Xi with three thousand horsemen to aid Yong in striking Gui; he utterly defeated him and pit-killed more than five thousand of Gui's surrendered soldiers.
idiomatic: When Murong Chui besieged Fu Pi at Ye and sent Ping Gui against Fu Jian's Youzhou inspector Wang Yong at Ji, Liu Kuren—still loyal to the titles Fu Jian had given him—sent his brother-in-law Gongsun Xi with three thousand horse to help Yong rout Gui and massacre more than five thousand of Gui's men who had surrendered.

literal: Seizing victory he drove far, advanced and held Tangcheng, and stood in stalemate with Chui's son Lin.
idiomatic: Riding the victory he drove deep, seized Tangcheng, and locked horns with Chui's son Lin.

literal: Kuren heard Xi had broken Gui and again was about to raise a great host to rescue Pi.
idiomatic: When Liu Kuren heard Xi had crushed Gui, he gathered a great army to relieve Fu Pi.

literal: He mobilized the armies of Yanmen, Shanggu, and Dai commanderies and halted at Fanzhi.
idiomatic: He called up the forces of Yanmen, Shanggu, and Dai and camped at Fanzhi.

literal: Earlier, Murong Wen and others had been due for relocation to Chang'an; they had fled into hiding with Kuren's tribe and constantly thought of returning east, but had no means.
idiomatic: Earlier Murong Wen and others, slated for resettlement in Chang'an, had taken refuge with Liu Kuren's tribe and longed to go east again but saw no way.

literal: At this levy they knew men were discontent; Wen and the rest therefore by night led the people of three commanderies to attack Kuren.
idiomatic: On this campaign they saw how little love the levy inspired; Wen and his party struck by night, leading men of three commanderies against Liu Kuren.

literal: Kuren hid in the horse stable; Wen seized and killed him.
idiomatic: Liu Kuren hid in the stable; Wen seized him and killed him.

literal: They took his swift horse and fled to Murong Chui.
idiomatic: They mounted his best horse and fled to Murong Chui.

literal: Gongsun Xi heard of the turmoil and fled from Tangcheng to the Dingling.
idiomatic: Gongsun Xi, hearing of the revolt, abandoned Tangcheng and fled to the Dingling.

literal: Kuren's younger brother Juan succeeded to take charge of state affairs.
idiomatic: Liu Kuren's younger brother Juan stepped in to govern the tribes.

literal: The White Division grandee Jiefu rebelled, [3] and Juan's strength could not subdue him.
idiomatic: Jiefu, grandee of the White Division, rebelled, [3] and Juan lacked the force to crush him.

literal: He therefore drew in Fu Jian's Inspector of Bingzhou Zhang Hao to strike Jiefu and break him.
idiomatic: He called in Fu Jian's Bingzhou inspector Zhang Hao, who defeated Jiefu.

literal: Juan again broke the Helan tribe at Shanwu and also attacked the Rouran sub-chieftain Feiwo at Yiqin Mountain, defeated him, and took several hundred thousand head of cattle and sheep.
idiomatic: Juan next routed the Helan at Shanwu and struck the Rouran sub-chief Feiwo at Yiqin Mountain, taking hundreds of thousands of cattle and sheep.

literal: Juan's second son Luo Chen was by nature alert and possessed wisdom and stratagem; he said to Juan: "In recent campaigns wherever we marched we were without match; the trouble in our vitals—I wish we would plan for it early.
idiomatic: Juan's second son Luo Chen was quick-witted and full of counsel; he told Juan, "Our armies have known no defeat—but the sickness is within. We should deal with it now."

literal: " Juan said: "Who is it?
idiomatic: " Juan asked, "Who?"

literal: " He said: "Cousin Xian is a man who can endure; his rebellion will come not in the morning then in the evening.
idiomatic: " He answered, "Cousin Xian is ruthless. His revolt is only a matter of time."

literal: " Juan did not take it to heart.
idiomatic: " Juan paid no heed.

literal: Afterward, when the herds were moved to pasture at Niuchuan, Kuren's son Xian indeed killed Juan and replaced him.
idiomatic: Later, when the herds were moved to Niuchuan, Liu Kuren's son Xian murdered Juan and usurped his place.

literal: Luo Chen fled to Taizu; the account is in the biography of the maternal kin.
idiomatic: Luo Chen fled to Taizu; the fuller account stands in the biography of the empresses' kin.

literal: Xian, original name Choufa, after killing Juan and replacing him also plotted rebellion; the words are in Taizu's annals.
idiomatic: Xian, whose birth name was Choufa, after killing Juan and seizing rule plotted treason as well; that story is told in Taizu's annals.

literal: When Taizu took the throne, Xian fled south from Shanwu to Mayi.
idiomatic: When Taizu was enthroned, Xian fled south from Shanwu toward Mayi.
